analysis.one_liner: Sets deadlines for gas pipeline permits, with approvals granted automatically if agencies miss them.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 252-165 in November 2013, but the Senate never voted on it and it expired with the 113th Congress in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to decide natural gas pipeline applications within 12 months, and required every other federal agency with a say — safety, environmental, land-management agencies — to approve or deny its permit within 90 days of FERC's final environmental review. If an agency ran out of time, the permit would automatically take effect 30 days later. The House passed it in November 2013; the Senate Commerce Committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that build and operate interstate natural gas pipelines gain the most: they would get a guaranteed 12-month decision on their FERC certificate and a 90-day clock on every other federal permit, with automatic approval if an agency misses its deadline. That removes the main leverage landowners, communities, and safety and environmental agencies have to slow or block a project — waiting out a slow agency review. Natural gas producers also gain, since faster pipeline approvals mean quicker routes to move gas to market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Natural gas pipeline developers and producers

how_it_helps.text: FERC must approve or deny a pipeline certificate within 12 months of receiving a complete application for a prefiled project, ending multi-year waits that add carrying costs for pipeline developers.

Every other federal agency with a required license, permit, or approval gets 90 days after FERC's final environmental document to act, with one 30-day extension available if the agency shows it would otherwise be forced to deny the permit.

If an agency neither approves nor denies a permit in time, the permit takes effect automatically 30 days after the deadline, and FERC must incorporate the agency's proffered conditions unless they conflict with the environmental document.
Faster, more predictable permitting lowers project costs and delay risk for pipeline builders and speeds gas delivery infrastructure to market.

analysis.who_pays: Communities along proposed pipeline routes, landowners, and the public bear the cost of compressed review: agencies would have only 90 days to complete safety, environmental, and landowner-impact reviews, and the automatic-approval default means an agency that cannot finish its work in time effectively loses the ability to say no at all. Any risk from an inadequately reviewed pipeline — safety failures, environmental damage, forced easements — falls on the people who live near it, not the pipeline company.

drawbacks.text: The automatic-approval default converts agency delay into a green light: an agency that needs more than 90 days (plus one 30-day extension) to review a pipeline's safety or environmental impact loses its ability to deny the permit entirely.

A motion to recommit that would have blocked the bill from taking effect unless FERC determined implementation would not adversely affect pipeline safety or inhibit communities from meaningfully engaging in siting failed 180-233, showing these concerns were raised and rejected on the floor.

The 90-day window applies to all federal permits simultaneously, forcing safety and land-management agencies to complete reviews on FERC's environmental-document timetable rather than their own — the single 30-day extension is the only relief, and FERC may grant it only if the agency shows it will otherwise be compelled to deny the permit.

All five Democratic floor amendments — including ones from Reps. Tonko, Castor, Speier, Jackson Lee, and Dingell — were rejected, so the bill passed without any of the community-participation or safety safeguards its critics proposed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Predictable permitting timelines have real value — multi-year federal reviews do delay infrastructure and add costs. But the design goes beyond setting deadlines: by making non-decision equivalent to approval, it removes the practical check that lets an agency deny a pipeline that fails its safety or environmental review, and it leaves route communities with 90 days to make their case. A bill that simply funded faster agency reviews would have captured most of the benefit without the default-approval risk; this one shifts the risk of an incomplete review onto the public.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 252-165 on November 21, 2013, but the Senate referred it to its Commerce Committee, which never voted on it, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Mike Pompeo on May 9, 2013 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which reported it amended by a 28-14 vote on November 18, 2013.
The House adopted a structured rule (H. Res. 420) allowing only specified amendments, and rejected all five Democratic amendments offered on the floor.

A motion to recommit with instructions — which would have prevented the bill from taking effect unless FERC found it would not harm pipeline safety or communities' ability to engage in siting — failed 180-233, with all voting Republicans against and 180 of 190 voting Democrats in favor.
Final passage passed 252-165, with 226 of 231 voting Republicans in favor and only 26 of 191 voting Democrats in favor.
The Senate received the bill on December 9, 2013 and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where it remained with no further action through the end of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pipeline-route communities, landowners, and federal review agencies are better off that it died, since they keep the full time agencies currently have to review pipeline safety and environmental impacts. Pipeline developers did not get the deadline-and-automatic-approval regime, but they also lost nothing — the existing permitting process, which they had operated under for decades, remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities and agencies keeping full review timelines

industries.industry: Natural gas pipeline developers and operators
industries.note: The bill gave these companies hard deadlines and, critically, automatic permit approval if any reviewing agency ran out of time — eliminating the practice of outlasting opposition through slow reviews. The industry's interest ran against communities and agencies that use review time as their main leverage. The bill died, so the industry remains under the existing process.

Faster pipeline approval means quicker takeaway capacity to move gas from producing regions to markets, which producers and gas consumers both benefit from. The cost of compressed safety and environmental review falls on pipeline-route communities rather than on producers.

The bill would have stripped these agencies' effective power to deny a pipeline permit by making failure to decide within 90 days equal to approval, and limited them to one 30-day extension. Their ability to complete thorough reviews is the public's main protection in pipeline siting.
